extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of American state government / comparative politics
extracted.subtask_description: Summarizes constitutional and statutory standards, procedural rules, and customary practices that govern U.S. state legislatures and executives (eligibility, suffrage, sessions, committees, vetoes, prohibited subjects, governor powers). Useful for understanding how state governments are structured and constrained.

rubrics_metrics.name: Senate partial renewal / continuity
rubrics_metrics.description: Senate is partially renewed, half its members going out when their two, or four, years have been completed, and a new half coming in.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This staggered renewal 'gives it a sense of continuity' which the House wants; continuity is presented as a deliberate design feature of the Senate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Age and basic eligibility requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: In some States a senator must have attained thirty years of age, in some a representative must have attained twenty-five. Other restrictions on eligibility, such as the exclusion of clergymen, that of salaried public officials, that of United States officials and members of Congress, and that of persons not resident in the electoral district, apply to both Houses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Residency rules are sometimes strict enough that a member ceasing to reside in the district for which he was elected loses his seat ipso facto.

rubrics_metrics.name: Residency / local-candidacy custom
rubrics_metrics.description: Nobody dreams of offering himself as a candidate for a place in which he does not reside; custom often restricts candidacy to residents of the district.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Custom (as opposed to law) can make reform difficult because customs must be unlearned over time; this habit prevents city-based educated men from entering state legislatures outside their local district.

rubrics_metrics.name: District size and election-area design
rubrics_metrics.description: Narrowing of election areas and allotting one senator or representative to each district tends to make the legislature inferior: 'The area of choice being smaller, inferior men are chosen.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contrasts historical multi-member/at-large elections (e.g., older Connecticut) where 'the best men of the whole State might be chosen' with later single-member districts that limit choice; multi-member districts may return better candidates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suffrage qualifications and exclusions
rubrics_metrics.description: Universal manhood suffrage, subject to certain disqualifications for crime (including bribery and polygamy) and the receipt of poor law relief, is the rule in nearly all the States. Ten States give the suffrage to women. Property and tax qualifications formerly existed in some States.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Rhode Island had property requirements until 1888; ten other states require payment of some state or county tax (poll tax), though parties often pay it for voters. These qualifications vary and have political effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Educational / literacy voting tests
rubrics_metrics.description: Some states require that the voter shall be able to read sections of the constitution or write his name; e.g., Massachusetts required reading the State Constitution in English and writing one's name; Connecticut required ability to read any section and to sustain a good moral character; Mississippi's registration requirement included being able to read any section or understand it when read to him or give a reasonable interpretation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These tests are often of little consequence where illiteracy is low, but have been used politically to exclude certain groups; examples noted for impact on excluding illiterate negroes while including illiterate whites.

rubrics_metrics.name: Federal franchise determined by state franchise
rubrics_metrics.description: By the Constitution of the United States, the right of suffrage in Federal or national elections is in each State that which the State confers on those who vote in the election of its more numerous House.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 14th Amendment incentive: representation (and thus weight in presidential elections) may be reduced proportionally to the number of adult male citizens disqualified, giving states a motive to widen the federal franchise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Variation in size of legislatures
rubrics_metrics.description: The number of members of the legislature varies greatly from State to State (examples: Delaware 17 senators; Minnesota 63; Delaware House 35; New Hampshire House 389).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Differences stem from historical/local reasons: New England's strong local feeling produced large assemblies; West and South preferred fewer representatives and lower pay.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legislative pay structure and session-length incentives
rubrics_metrics.description: Members receive the same salary in both Houses. Pay is sometimes fixed annually (from $150 to $1500), more frequently paid by the day ($1 to $8 per day), plus mileage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Low/partial pay and per diem systems encourage limiting session length; some states reduce or cease daily pay after a certain number of days to check prolonged sessions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Session frequency and extraordinary sessions
rubrics_metrics.description: Legislatures were formerly annual; now sessions are biennial in all States except some (e.g., Alabama and Mississippi quadrennial; Massachusetts, Rhode Island, New York, New Jersey, South Carolina, Georgia annual). Governors generally may summon extraordinary sessions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some biennial legislatures hold adjourned sessions in off years; provisions for daily pay often do not apply to extraordinary sessions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Origination of bills and money-bill rule
rubrics_metrics.description: Bills may originate in either House, save that in most States money bills must originate in the House of Representatives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The rule is a historical survival from English practice; State Senates may amend or reject money bills like other bills.

rubrics_metrics.name: Senate special powers (impeachment & confirmations)
rubrics_metrics.description: A State Senate sits as a court under oath for the trial of State officials impeached by the House, and in many States has the power of confirming or rejecting appointments by the governor ('go into executive session').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Power is important where governors nominate higher judges; examples: New York impeachments tried by Senate and judges of Court of Appeals; Nebraska by Supreme Court judges.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quorum and attendance enforcement
rubrics_metrics.description: Legal quorum usually fixed by the Constitution at a majority of the whole number of members elected, though smaller numbers may adjourn and compel attendance; some constitutions fix quorum at two-thirds or specify a number.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quorum rules vary and are constitutionally set; houses may compel attendance of absent members.

rubrics_metrics.name: Committee-centred legislative process
rubrics_metrics.description: Both Houses do most of their work by committees; committees are usually chosen by the Speaker or President, though houses may vary composition; committees settle form of bills and often decide their fate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Committee proceedings are rarely reported; in some states citizens may appear and give evidence before committees (e.g., Massachusetts), which can yield 'excellent results'. Lobby influence is noted as usually pernicious.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparency / secret sessions and public evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Both Houses sit with open doors, but most State Constitutions empower them to exclude strangers when secrecy required; some provision against secret sessions (Idaho).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Public committee hearings with reporters make proceedings resemble public meetings; many constitutions direct plain wording and avoidance of technical terms (Idaho, Indiana, Oregon) and forbid adopting laws by general reference (Louisiana).

rubrics_metrics.name: Governor veto power and override thresholds
rubrics_metrics.description: All States but one (North Carolina) require bills to be submitted to the governor and permit him to return it with objections; to pass a bill over the veto different states require varying majorities (enumerated: e.g., in twenty-seven States a majority of two-thirds of all the members elected; other permutations listed).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The book lists the specific distributions: one State (Connecticut) majority in each House; eight States majority of all members elected; three States three-fifths of all members elected; eight States two-thirds of all members present; twenty-seven States two-thirds of all members elected; Massachusetts and Virginia have hybrid rules — these rules act as safeguards and escape routes from deadlocks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constitutional exclusions of subject-matter (prohibited statutes)
rubrics_metrics.description: Exclusions of subjects from legislative competence: statutes inconsistent with democratic principles (e.g., granting titles of nobility, favouring one religion, creating property qualification for suffrage or office); statutes against public policy (e.g., lotteries, impairing contracts, incorporating or permitting incorporation of banks or state holding of bank stock); statutes special or local in application; statutes increasing state or local debt beyond a limited amount.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some state constitutions (Missouri 1875; Montana and North Dakota 1889; Mississippi 1890; Oklahoma 1907) enumerate long lists; Oklahoma forbids special legislation on twenty-eight topics. Debt limits often fixed in proportion to valuation of taxable property.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedural restrictions on lawmaking
rubrics_metrics.description: Directions as to particular forms and times: required majorities for certain bills (esp. appropriations); method of taking votes (roll call and record); intervals between each reading of a measure; reading bills publicly and at full length; sending bills to committee and prescribing its mode of action; preventing secret sessions (Idaho); preventing acts from taking effect until a certain time after adjournment; prohibiting change of bill purpose during passage; requiring single subject and its expression in the bill title; forbidding re-enacting/amending/incorporating former acts by mere reference to their title.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Idaho, Indiana, Oregon direct plain wording; Louisiana forbids adopting a system/code by general reference and requires reciting provisions at length. Violations of these procedural rules may render statutes void as inconsistent with the Constitution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Invalidity of statutes violating prohibitions or forms
rubrics_metrics.description: Where statutes have been passed by a legislature upon a prohibited subject, or where the prescribed forms have been transgressed or omitted, the statute will be held void so far as inconsistent with the Constitution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Constitutional judicial review enforces these limits; 'so far as inconsistent' indicates partial invalidation possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legislative resolutions on foreign affairs (resoluting)
rubrics_metrics.description: Although State legislatures have no concern with foreign affairs, they do not abstain from passing resolutions expressing sympathy or displeasure; 'the passion for what is called
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such resolutions are irregular but usually innocuous and may serve electioneering purposes by appealing to sections of state voters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Debate reporting and influence on oratory vs management
rubrics_metrics.description: Debates in these bodies are seldom well reported and sometimes not at all; as a result speeches are generally short and practical, and committee work means 'talent for intrigue or management usually counts for more than debating power.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lack of reporting reduces rhetorical incentive; committee work privileges management skills and can shield conduct from constituent scrutiny.

rubrics_metrics.name: Governor election, term, salary, and eligibility limits
rubrics_metrics.description: The governor is elected by the people (directly). Terms vary: 23 States four years, 1 State three years (New Jersey), 22 States two years, 2 States one year (Massachusetts and Rhode Island). Salary varies ($12,000 to $2,500 examples). Some states limit re-eligibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Variation reflects state choice; absence of tradition may allow multiple terms where not limited; salary and term length affect executive incentives and conduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Governor executive powers (pardon, militia, appointments)
rubrics_metrics.description: Governor charged with seeing laws are faithfully administered; power of reprieving and pardoning offenders (sometimes limited, e.g., cannot pardon treason or conviction on impeachment; Vermont cannot pardon for murder); commander-in-chief of State armed forces, may embody militia, repel invasion, suppress insurrection; may appoint some officials (often requiring Senate approval).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some constitutions impose restrictions witnessing distrust of the power; examples of states with State police forces (Massachusetts, Pennsylvania, Michigan, New York, Delaware) illustrate executive tools for order and election supervision. Patronage value of governor is limited because many important offices are directly elected.

rubrics_metrics.name: Governor legislative interaction (recommendations, information, veto)
rubrics_metrics.description: Governor may require information from other executive officials, is bound to communicate to the legislature his views regarding the condition of the commonwealth, may recommend measures, and in some states present estimates; governor has veto power in all States but North Carolina.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Governor is not expected to frame and present bills but often influences legislation by having measures introduced that embody his recommendations; the veto is a chief tool by which a governor is judged and often kills measures because overriding majorities are difficult to obtain.
